title: Zero-, One-, Two- and Three-Address Formats
quickIdea: How many operands an instruction names decides how many instructions a statement costs. The more addresses per instruction, the fewer instructions - and the more bits per instruction.
remember: 0-address: operands are on a stack, pushed and popped. 1-address: one operand, the other is the implied accumulator. 2-address: one operand is also the destination. 3-address: two sources and a separate destination.
An address field may name a memory location or a processor register. It may not name an implied accumulator, because an implied operand is by definition not written down.
Fewer addresses means a shorter instruction but a longer program. This is a straight trade, not an improvement.
Typical counts for X = (A + B) * (C + D): 3 three-address, 6 two-address, 7 one-address, 8 zero-address.
Two-address arithmetic destroys one source operand, so a compiler must copy it first if it is needed again.
The three-address form is what makes expression evaluation short; the bit cost of three address fields is why it is not universal.

example.prompt: Count the instructions needed for X = (A + B) * (C + D) in one-address and two-address form.
example.work: One-address (accumulator): LOAD A; ADD B; STORE T; LOAD C; ADD D; MUL T; STORE X - 7 instructions. Two-address: MOV R1, A; ADD R1, B; MOV R2, C; ADD R2, D; MUL R1, R2; MOV X, R1 - 6 instructions. Three-address would be ADD R1, A, B; ADD R2, C, D; MUL X, R1, R2 - 3.
example.answer: 7 in one-address form, 6 in two-address form, 3 in three-address form.

gateAngle: GATE CSE 2015 Set 1 Q.8 asks what a single address field of a three-address format may specify, and the answer is memory or register but never an implied accumulator - the question is testing whether you know that 'three-address' is about fields, not about a machine with three registers. The instruction-count comparison is the standard companion and appears in the textbook exercises rather than in a CSE paper.

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: In a two-address machine, how many instructions does X = A + B + C + D take, and how many temporaries are needed?
variations.answer: Four instructions - MOV R1, A; ADD R1, B; ADD R1, C; ADD R1, D - and no temporaries.
variations.why: Two-address form can accumulate into one register when the expression is a chain of additions, so no temporary is needed. A tree-shaped expression such as (A+B)*(C+D) does need one.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: Why can a zero-address machine evaluate (A+B)*(C+D) with no temporaries?
variations.answer: Because the stack itself holds the intermediate values: after pushing A and B and adding, the partial sum is on the stack, and the second sum goes above it.
variations.why: The stack is the temporary store. That is why stack machines have such short opcodes and such long programs.

variations.label: PREDICTED VARIATION
variations.question: A three-address format has three 8-bit address fields and a 4-bit opcode. How wide must the word be, and what does that say about three-address designs?
variations.answer: 28 bits. Three 8-bit fields reach only 256 locations each, so three-address designs are usually paired with a register file rather than a large memory.
variations.why: This is precisely why real three-address machines name registers in two fields and memory in none.

trap.what: Assuming a three-address instruction must name three memory addresses.
trap.why: The address field may hold a register number. In a load-store machine all three fields are registers and memory never appears in the instruction.
trap.counterexample: ADD R1, R2, R3 has three address fields and touches no memory at all. Only a load or a store instruction reaches memory.

check.question: How many instructions does X = A * B take in zero-address form?
check.answer: Four: PUSH A; PUSH B; MUL; POP X.
check.explanation: Two pushes put the operands on the stack, MUL replaces the top two by their product, and POP stores the result. A one-address machine needs three: LOAD A; MUL B; STORE X.
